note: Position paper defining levels of contamination and calling for per benchmark measurement, widely cited in later standards work.
title: NLP Evaluation in trouble: On the Need to Measure LLM Data Contamination for each Benchmark
explain_beginner: Large language models are being tested on standard benchmark datasets to measure how well they work. However, researchers discovered a serious problem: sometimes the test data used to evaluate these models was already included in their training data. This creates fake high scores that don't reflect real performance. The paper warns that this contamination is widespread but hard to detect, leading scientists to draw wrong conclusions about which models actually work best.
explain_business: Organizations relying on published LLM benchmarks to select models face a hidden risk: performance claims may be artificially inflated by data leakage rather than genuine capability. This paper identifies that standard evaluation practices lack verification mechanisms, potentially leading to poor procurement decisions. Investment in contamination detection and benchmark integrity becomes a competitive advantage, while ignoring this issue risks deploying models that underperform in real applications compared to published metrics.
explain_practitioner: The authors identify data contamination as a critical validity threat in LLM evaluation, where test set exposure during training inflates benchmark performance metrics. They propose a taxonomy of contamination levels and argue for systematic per-benchmark detection mechanisms, combining automatic and semi-automatic approaches. The key finding emphasizes that contamination severity remains unmeasured across most studies, necessitating community-wide measurement protocols to prevent spurious performance claims and ensure reproducible, scientifically sound model comparisons.
